teacher_note: Draft for teacher review. Before a classroom pilot, review the course (especially Who decides?, Many voices and Mesa Verde, around 1280) with Crow Canyon's education team or a tribal cultural office. No tribe has endorsed this course.

lessons.title: Clues, not treasure
lessons.brief: Archaeologists read the past from what people left behind. Your Field Director is your CAPCOM on the dig. The Lab is your Houston: results come back later.

steps.prompt: What is an archaeologist mostly looking for?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: Clues. A broken pot can say more than gold.
steps.reveal: Clues. A broken pot can say more than gold.

steps.prompt: Find Mesa Verde National Park, in the southwest corner of Colorado.
steps.hint: Southwest Colorado, near the Four Corners.
steps.success: That's it. Nearly 5,000 sites are protected here.

steps.prompt: Which of these is evidence you could check yourself?

options.label: A roof beam with a tree-ring date

steps.hint: Evidence can be measured again by someone else.
steps.success: Right. Anyone can re-measure a dated beam.

steps.prompt: Name the field that studies the past through what people left.
steps.hint: It starts with arch.
steps.success: Archaeology. Clues first, then claims.

steps.prompt: On a park trail you spot a piece of broken pottery. What do you do?

options.label: Photograph it and leave it
options.reply: That's the call. Where it lies is part of the clue. Tell a ranger.

options.label: Take it home to keep it safe
options.reply: It feels safe, but once moved it loses its place in the story. Leave it, report it.

options.label: Hide it so nobody takes it
options.reply: Kind thought, but moving it erases where it was. Photograph it and tell a ranger.

law.text: Leave it where you found it, take a picture, and show a park ranger where it is.

lessons.title: Layers tell time
lessons.brief: Soil piles up like pages in a book: the bottom page was written first. This trench is a teaching drawing, not a real site.

steps.prompt: In undisturbed ground, which layer is oldest?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: The bottom. That's the law of superposition.
steps.reveal: The bottom. That's the law of superposition.

steps.prompt: This trench cuts an old pithouse. Order its layers from oldest to youngest.
steps.hint: Start at the bottom. A pit is as young as the layers it cuts.
steps.success: Right. Floor, a fire, the roof fell, then someone dug a pit.
steps.do: Tap the layers oldest first, or say them

steps.prompt: A pit cuts down through three layers. The pit is...

options.label: The same age as the middle one

steps.hint: Could you dig a hole through a layer that wasn't there yet?
steps.success: Younger. Whatever cuts a layer came after it.

steps.prompt: What is the study of layers called?
steps.hint: It starts with strat, like strata.
steps.success: Stratigraphy. Layers are a timeline you can read.

steps.prompt: Put the dig steps in order.
steps.hint: Find it, photograph it, then bag it.
steps.success: That's a clean record.

facts.text: Law of Superposition: in any undisturbed sequence of deposits, the deeper layers are older than those above them.

source.title: Glossary (U.S. National Park Service) [Southwest archeology glossary]

facts.text: Younger rocks or structures cut across older ones: a cut is younger than what it cuts.

lessons.title: Dating the past
lessons.brief: A roof beam can tell you the year its tree was cut. Like Houston, the Lab answers after a delay: radiocarbon results take days or weeks.

steps.prompt: Can a roof beam give the exact year its tree was cut?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: Yes. In the Southwest, tree rings can give the exact year.
steps.reveal: Yes. In the Southwest, tree rings can give the exact year.

steps.prompt: Slide this beam until its rings match the master pattern. Then say its outer year.
steps.hint: Match the very narrow rings first.
steps.success: 1275. The same year the park reports for a Long House beam.
steps.do: Slide the beam until the bars match, then lock in

steps.prompt: For trees that need rain, a wide ring usually means a year that was...
steps.hint: More water, more growth.
steps.success: Wet. Rainy years grow wide rings.

steps.prompt: The Lab dates a piece of charcoal by radiocarbon. What comes back?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: A range of years, like 1220 to 1290. Rings can give the exact year.
steps.reveal: A range of years, like 1220 to 1290. Rings can give the exact year.

steps.prompt: Tree-ring dating has a long name. Say it.
steps.hint: Dendro means tree. Chronology means time.
steps.success: Dendrochronology. Tree time.

lessons.title: Things people left
lessons.brief: Everyday things tell how people lived. Where a thing is found matters as much as the thing.

steps.prompt: A flat stone slab and a hand-sized stone. What were they for?

steps.success: Grinding corn. They are a mano and a metate.

The big flat stone it rubs on?

rounds.prompt: A broken piece of a clay pot?

steps.success: All four. A midden is a great record of daily life.

lessons.title: Who decides?
lessons.brief: US law protects sites on public and tribal land. It also says who must be asked first.

steps.prompt: Can anyone dig on public land if they are careful?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: No. Digging on public or Indian lands needs a permit.
steps.reveal: No. Digging on public or Indian lands needs a permit.

steps.prompt: Match each law to what it does.

rounds.prompt: The first US law to protect sites on federal lands?
Makes digging without a permit a crime?
Agencies must weigh a project's effects on historic places?
Returns ancestors and sacred objects to tribes?

steps.hint: One law at a time.
steps.success: Four laws, one idea: ask before you dig.

steps.prompt: A road is planned across a recorded site. What happens first?

lessons.title: Many voices
lessons.brief: The people of Mesa Verde moved south. Their descendants live today, and they describe these places in their own words.

steps.prompt: What happened to the people of Mesa Verde around 1300?

options.label: They moved south; their descendants live today

steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: They moved. Today's Pueblo and Hopi people are their direct descendants.
steps.reveal: They moved. Today's Pueblo and Hopi people are their direct descendants.

steps.prompt: A Pueblo ranger at Mesa Verde says where her people live now. Where?
steps.hint: Read her words above.
steps.success: In 21 Pueblos in New Mexico, Arizona and Texas.

quote.text: I would like visitors to know that we didn't just leave and disappear. When the ancestors left Mesa Verde, they migrated toward the south, where we still live today in 21 Pueblos in the states of New Mexico, Arizona, and Texas.

lessons.title: Mesa Verde, around 1280
lessons.unit: Case study: drought, tree rings, migration
lessons.brief: Join the clues: rings, layers and people's own histories. There is no single answer here, only evidence.

steps.prompt: Very narrow tree rings across the late 1200s suggest...
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: Drought. Researchers call 1276 to 1299 the Great Drought.
steps.reveal: Drought. Researchers call 1276 to 1299 the Great Drought.

steps.prompt: Order Mesa Verde's homes, oldest first.
steps.hint: Partly underground came first.
steps.success: About 550 to 1300: pithouses, pueblos, cliffs, then south.

steps.prompt: The last tree-ring date in the region is...
steps.hint: Close to the Long House beam.
steps.success: 1281. By 1300, people had moved south.

steps.prompt: A classmate says one cause explains the move. You...

options.label: Ask for more evidence
options.reply: Good science. Drought, crop failure and social change are all discussed.

options.label: Agree: it was only drought

lessons.title: Moonrise at Chimney Rock
lessons.brief: The Moon course meets this one in southwest Colorado. At Chimney Rock, the Moon sometimes rises between two stone spires.

steps.prompt: How often does the Moon rise between Chimney Rock's two spires?
steps.hint: Any guess is fine.
steps.success: About every 18.6 years, at the major lunar standstill.
steps.reveal: About every 18.6 years, at the major lunar standstill.

steps.prompt: Find Chimney Rock National Monument in southwest Colorado.
steps.hint: East of Mesa Verde, in the San Juan National Forest.
steps.success: There. The two spires are Chimney Rock and Companion Rock.

steps.prompt: After the 2024 and 2025 viewings, when is the next major standstill?
steps.hint: Add 18.6 years to 2025.
steps.success: 2044. Mark your calendar.
